DEPARTMENT 205 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 23SMCV00558    Hearing Date: September 23, 2026    Dept: 205

HEARING DATE:  September 23, 2026 

JUDGE/DEPT:  Moreton/Beverly Hills, 205 

CASE NAME: Ando Hacopian v. 27715 LLC, et al. 

CASE NUMBER:  23SMCV00558 

 

COMP. FILED: February 7, 2023 

 

 

 

PROCEEDINGS: REQUEST FOR ENTRY OF DEFAULT JUDGMENT 

MOVING PARTY: VIG Private Lending, Inc., Val Serbryany as trustee of the Val Serbryany Family Trust, and 27715 LLC 

RESPONDING PARTY: Edmond Aslan and Aslan Construction, Inc. 

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a fraud case.  Plaintiff Ando Hacopian’s company, Hacopian Design & Development Group, LLC (“Hacopian LLC”) owned the real property located at 27715 Pacific Coast Highway, Malibu, CA 90265 (“the Property”)..  Hacopian LLC’s business was to buy properties, and to remodel or construct homes on the properties for purposes of resale.   

Plaintiff acquired two loans from Defendant VIG Private Lending, Inc. and the Val Serbryany Family Trust, one to help purchase the property ($2 million) and another for construction costs ($3 million) including an interest reserve loan to help pay for the interest payments during the construction period when Plaintiff may not have sufficient cash flow.   

Plaintiff defaulted on the payments to VIG as well as other lender(s), and as a result, the Property was sold in non-judicial foreclosure.  Title to the Property was conveyed to 27715 LLC.  VIG is the controlling member of 27715 LLC.  Vladimir Valsky is the manager of 27715 LLC.  

Plaintiff sued VIG, 27715 LLC, and VIG’s member (Vladimir Valsky) claiming that they had falsely promised Plaintiff that 27715 LLC “would sell and transfer all membership interests in Plaintiff for payment of $4,800,000.”  The complaint alleged claims for promissory fraud, specific performance and breach of contract.   

Defendants then countersued Plaintiff and his company, Hacopian LLC for breach of written guaranty, fraud, mortgage fraud, negligence and restitution.  Defendants’ suit also named other defendants, including (as relevant here) Edmond Aslan, Aslan Construction, Inc. (the Aslan Cross-Defendants).  All claims have been settled except for those between the Cross-Complainants and the Aslan Cross-Defendants.   

The Aslan Cross-Defendants were hired to do the construction on the Property.  After the foreclosure sale and upon Cross-Complainants' possession of the Property, Cross-Complainants claim they discovered many problems with the construction, including that: (1) many of the construction items which had been represented by Aslan as completed at the Property during the Loans were not done; (2) other construction items had been completed without proper completion of inspections by the City of Malibu, leading to the need to tear out much of the construction to allow inspection; (3) the work performed by Aslan Construction on the Property was negligently performed;. (4) much of the material supplied for the construction at the Property was substandard; (5) the amount disbursed from the Construction Loan to the Aslan Cross-Defendants were far in excess of what it would have cost for the scope and quality of work and materials that were actually used and completed at the Property. 

Cross-Complainants sued the Aslan Cross-Defendants for negligence, restitution and fraud.  The Complaint sought damages in an amount to be proven at trial but which exceeds $250,000.  (Cross-Complaint ¶¶ 81, 93, 96.) 

Cross-Complainants filed proofs of service indicating that the Aslan Cross-Defendants had been substitute served on March 2, 2026.  The proofs included a very detailed declaration from the registered process server, William Sera.  The Aslan Cross-Defendants did not respond within the statutory deadline.     

On January 21, 2026, following Cross-Complainants' filing of a Request for Entry of Default, the Clerk of the Court entered default against the Aslan Cross-Defendants.  The Aslan Cross-Defendants answered after the default had already been entered. The Aslan Cross-Defendants then filed motions to vacate default/default judgment and to quash the service of summons.  The Court denied the motions.  This hearing is on Cross-Complainants' request for entry of default judgment.   

Cross-Complainants had previously requested default judgment in the amount of $5,815,524, which the Court denied because it was in excess of the amount sought in the Complaint.  Cross-Complainants' new request for default judgment seeks $250,000 in damages.   

REQUEST FOR RELIEF 

Cross-Complainants seek a total of $250,000 in damages.   

 

ANALYSIS 

 

Cross-Complainants declare via the declaration of Vladimir Valsky, the President of VIG that the Aslan Cross-Defendants’ negligence and fraud resulted in damages of $5,815,524.00, although they only seek $250,000.  (Valsky Decl. ¶¶12-13.)  Valsky attests that the Cross-Complainants' contractors found many issues with the Aslan Cross-Defendants’ construction.   

The contractors (1) determined that $1,228,524 in work and materials that were paid for through the construction loan was not actually completed and installed by the Aslan Cross-Defendants; (2) other construction items had been completed without proper inspections by the City of Malibu, which resulted in the contractors having to tear down the construction to allow city inspection and $465,000 in extra work, material costs, and permit costs; (3) many areas of the work performed by the Aslan Cross-Defendants were visibly defective, consisted of poor construction, were incomplete, were uninspected, and were below industry standards, requiring the work to be redone which cost $170,000; (4) many items of material supplied for the construction at the Property were substandard and were not what was represented to have been used in the documentation for the draw requests, reducing “value of the completed project” by $3,000,000, and (5) all of the above-described deficiencies has caused a delay to the completion of the project for 8 months which resulted in total delay costs of $952,000.  (Valsky Decl. ¶¶9-10.)   

Valsky does not submit any evidence in support of the above.  There are no invoices or other documents which would reflect amounts paid by Cross-Complainants.  Further, to the extent Valsky relies on the contractors’ statements, they are hearsay.   

While Code of Civil Procedure section 585 does give the court discretion to “permit the use of affidavits, in lieu of personal testimony, as to all or any part of the evidence or proof required or permitted to be offered, received, or heard in those cases,” it specifically requires that “[t]he facts stated in the affidavit or affidavits shall be within the personal knowledge of the affiant and shall be set forth with particularity, and each affidavit shall show affirmatively that the affiant, if sworn as a witness, can testify competently thereto.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 585, subd. (d), italics added.)  

Damages must be proven with admissible evidence as part of the default judgment application or in a default judgment prove-up hearing.  (Kim v. Westmoore, 201 Cal.App.4th at 288 (despite default, damages require proof).) 

CONCLUSION AND ORDER 

For the foregoing reasons, Cross-Complainants' Request for Default Judgment is DENIED without prejudice.  The Order to Show Cause Re: Entry of Default Judgment is continued to January 8, 2027 at 8:30 a.m. 

Case Number: 25SMCV00582    Hearing Date: September 23, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

 

STEPHANIE CICERI, et al.,  

 

Plaintiffs, 

v. 

 

GLOBAL INTEGRITY REALTYCORPORATION, et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  25SMCV00582 

  Hearing Date:  September 23, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  PLAINTIFFS' MOTION TO VACATE  

  RULING ON DEFENDANT’s MOTION  

  FOR JUDGMENT ON THE PLEADINGS  

  and reset hearing 

 

 

 

This hearing is on Plaintiffs’ motion to vacate the Court’s order granting Defendant’s motion for judgment on the pleadings and to reset the hearing on the motion.  The motion seeks mandatory relief pursuant to Cal. Civ. Proc. Code section 473(b).  Plaintiffs argue that their counsel failed to appear at the hearing on the motion for judgment on the pleadings because of a car emergency involving his son, and counsel was not able to reach his co-counsel.   

Section 473(b) states (in relevant part): “[T]he court shall, whenever an application for relief is made no more than six months after entry of judgment, is in proper form, and is accompanied by an attorney's sworn affidavit attesting to his or her mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect, vacate any (1) resulting default entered by the clerk against his or her client, and which will result in entry of a default judgment, or (2) resulting default judgment or dismissal entered against his or her client, unless the court finds that the default or dismissal was not in fact caused by the attorney's mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect.” (§ 473(b), italics added.) 

Thus, for mandatory relief to be granted to a plaintiff, (1) the relief must be sought within six months after entry of judgment, (2) be accompanied by an attorney’s sworn affidavit, (3) involve a dismissal, and (4) the dismissal must be caused by the attorney’s mistake, inadvertence, surprise or neglect.   

Here, there has been no entry of judgment, and accordingly, Plaintiffs’ filing of the motion to vacate is timely.  Plaintiffs’ motion is accompanied by a sworn affidavit by their counsel which Plaintiffs argue support a showing of excusable neglect.  In any event, pursuant to 473(b), Plaintiffs are not required to show excusable neglect.  The range of attorney conduct for which relief can be granted in the mandatory provision is broader than that in the discretionary provision and includes inexcusable neglect. (Tackett v. City of Huntington Beach (1994) 22 Cal.App.4th 60, 65 [“a mea culpa declaration by an attorney establishing that a default, default judgment, or dismissal was entered against his or her client as the result of attorney neglect deprives the trial court of discretion to deny relief, even without a showing that the neglect was excusable.”].)  

As to whether there has been a “dismissal”, numerous Court of Appeal decisions have limited the reach of Section 473(b) as it relates to relief from a “dismissal.” Although the statutory language “on its face, ‘affords relief from unspecified ‘dismissal’ caused by attorney neglect, our courts have, through judicial construction, prevented it from being used indiscriminately by plaintiffs’ attorneys as a ‘perfect escape hatch’ [citations] to undo dismissals of civil cases.” 

For example, “[c]ourts have held the mandatory provision is inapplicable to voluntary dismissals [citation] and dismissals for lapsing of the statute of limitations [citation], failure to serve a complaint in a timely manner [citation], failure to prosecute [citation], and failure to file an amended complaint after a demurrer has been sustained with leave to amend.” (Gotschall, supra, 96 Cal.App.4th at 483–484; see also Urban Wildlands, 10 Cal.App.5th at 999 [listing additional cases declining to apply mandatory provision, including in summary judgment context].) 

As to demurrers, however, the California Court of Appeal has held that the sustaining of a demurrer is a “dismissal” for purposes of Section 473(b).  (Pangini v. Union Bank, N.A. (2018) 28 Cal.App.5th 298, 304.)  Relying on the definition of “dismissal” in section 581, the Pangini court held that “[a]n action may be dismissed” after a demurrer to the complaint is sustained without leave to amend and either party moves for dismissal. (§ 581, subds. (b), (f)(1).)   

As a motion for judgment on the pleadings is the functional equivalent of a demurrer, the Court concludes that the granting of a motion for judgment on the pleadings also constitutes a dismissal under section 473(b).  (Weil & Brown, Jr., RUTTER: California Practice Guide - Civil Procedure Before Trial, ¶7:275, p. 7(1) - 85 (2020) (“A motion for judgment on the pleadings has the same function as a general demurrer but is made after the time for demurrer has expired.”); Templo v. State of California (2018) 24 Cal.App.5th 730, 735 (“A motion for judgment on the pleadings is equivalent to a demurrer ...”).) 

Turning to the last requirement for mandatory relief, the Court must consider whether the Court’s order on the motion for judgment on the pleadings was a result of counsel’s failure to appear at the hearing.  The Court concludes that it was not.  The Court’s ruling was based on the merits of the motion, and not because of the nonappearance of Plaintiffs’ counsel.  Vacating the ruling on the motion for judgment on the pleadings and re-setting a hearing on the motion would be a complete waste of the Court’s resources and the parties’ time.  Accordingly, the Court DENIES the motion to vacate and to reset hearing.

Judge of the Superior Court 

Case Number: 25SMCV00751    Hearing Date: September 23, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

 

CHRISTOPHER BELTRAN, et al.,  

 

Plaintiffs, 

v. 

 

GLOBAL INTEGRITY REALTYCORPORATION, et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  25SMCV00751 

  Hearing Date:  September 23, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  PLAINTIFFS' MOTION TO VACATE  

  RULING ON DEFENDANT’s demurrer  

  to first amended complaint and  

  reset hearing 

 

 

 

This hearing is on Plaintiffs’ motion to vacate the Court’s order sustaining Defendant’s demurrer to Plaintiffs’ first amended complaint and reset the hearing on the demurrer.  The motion seeks mandatory relief pursuant to Cal. Civ. Proc. Code section 473(b).  Plaintiffs argue that their counsel failed to appear at the hearing on the demurrer because of a car emergency involving his son, and counsel was not able to reach his co-counsel.   

Section 473(b) states (in relevant part): “[T]he court shall, whenever an application for relief is made no more than six months after entry of judgment, is in proper form, and is accompanied by an attorney's sworn affidavit attesting to his or her mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect, vacate any (1) resulting default entered by the clerk against his or her client, and which will result in entry of a default judgment, or (2) resulting default judgment or dismissal entered against his or her client, unless the court finds that the default or dismissal was not in fact caused by the attorney's mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or neglect.” (§ 473(b), italics added.) 

Thus, for mandatory relief to be granted to a plaintiff, the relief (1) must be sought within six months after entry of judgment, (2) be accompanied by an attorney’s sworn affidavit, (3) involve a dismissal, and (4) the dismissal must be caused by the attorney’s mistake, inadvertence, surprise or neglect.   

Here, there has been no entry of judgment, and accordingly, Plaintiffs’ filing of the motion to vacate is timely.  Plaintiffs’ motion is accompanied by a sworn affidavit by their counsel which Plaintiffs argue support a showing of excusable neglect.  In any event, pursuant to 473(b), Plaintiffs are not required to show excusable neglect.  The range of attorney conduct for which relief can be granted in the mandatory provision is broader than that in the discretionary provision and includes inexcusable neglect. (Tackett v. City of Huntington Beach (1994) 22 Cal.App.4th 60, 65 [27 Cal. Rptr. 2d 133] [“a mea culpa declaration by an attorney establishing that a default, default judgment, or dismissal was entered against his or her client as the result of attorney neglect deprives the trial court of discretion to deny relief, even without a showing that the neglect was excusable.”].)  

As to whether there has been a “dismissal”, numerous Court of Appeal decisions have limited the reach of Section 473(b) as it relates to relief from a “dismissal.” Although the statutory language “on its face, ‘affords relief from unspecified ‘dismissal’ caused by attorney neglect, our courts have, through judicial construction, prevented it from being used indiscriminately by plaintiffs’ attorneys as a ‘perfect escape hatch’ [citations] to undo dismissals of civil cases.” 

For example, “[c]ourts have held the mandatory provision is inapplicable to voluntary dismissals [citation] and dismissals for lapsing of the statute of limitations [citation], failure to serve a complaint in a timely manner [citation], failure to prosecute [citation], and failure to file an amended complaint after a demurrer has been sustained with leave to amend.” (Gotschall, supra, 96 Cal.App.4th at 483–484; see also Urban Wildlands, 10 Cal.App.5th at 999 [listing additional cases declining to apply mandatory provision, including in summary judgment context].) 

As to demurrers, however, the California Court of Appeal has held that the sustaining of a demurrer is a “dismissal” for purposes of Section 473(b).  (Pangini v. Union Bank, N.A. (2018) 28 Cal.App.5th 298, 304.)  The Pangini court cited to section 581 (“Dismissal; definitions”) which states that “[a]n action may be dismissed,” including “after a demurrer to the complaint is sustained without leave to amend and either party moves for dismissal.” (§ 581, subds. (b), (f)(1).)  

Turning to the last requirement for mandatory relief, the Court must consider whether the Court’s order on the demurrer was a result of counsel’s failure to appear at the hearing.  The Court concludes that it was not.  The Court’s ruling was based on the merits of the demurrer, and not because of the nonappearance of Plaintiffs’ counsel.  Vacating the ruling and re-setting a hearing on the demurrer would be a complete waste of the Court’s and parties’ time.  Accordingly, the Court DENIES the motion to vacate.

Case Number: 25SMCV01212    Hearing Date: September 23, 2026    Dept: 205

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District 

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

 

DAVID LANCE ARMSTRONG, 

  

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

655 KELTON LP, et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  25SMCV01212 

  

  Hearing Date:  September 23, 2026 

 

 

  [TENTATIVE] ORDER RE: 

  PLAINTIFF’S MOTIONS TO COMPEL  

  RESPONSES TO FORM  

  INTERROGATORIES, SET ONE;  

  SPECIAL INTERROGATORIES, SET ONE;  

  DEMAND FOR PRODUCTION, SET ONE;  

  MOTION TO DEEM ADMITTED  

  REQUESTS FOR ADMISSION AND  

  REQUEST FOR SANCTIONS, AGAINST  

  DEFENDANT 655 KELTON, LP 

 

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

 

This is a slip and fall case.  Plaintiff David Lance Armstrong was delivering food to an apartment building located at 655 Kelton Avenue, Westwood, California when he slipped on a wet substance and fell.   

He has sued three defendants: 655 Kelton, LP, Amir Development Co. and WA Management, LLC.  Plaintiff claims that they were on notice of the dangerous condition and failed to warn or remedy.  His complaint alleges two causes of action for negligence and premises liability.   

On November 18, 2025, Plaintiff propounded four sets of discovery requests on 655 Kelton LP: Form Interrogatories (set one) (FROGs); Special Interrogatories (set one) (SROGs); Requests for Production of Documents (set one) (RFPs), and Requests for Admissions (set one) (RFAs).  The discovery requests were served by e-mail.  Responses were due by December 30, 2025, 30 days plus 2 court days for email service.   

655 Kelton LP did not respond within the statutory deadline.  Many months later, on July 30, 2026, Plaintiff’s counsel emailed defense counsel regarding the overdue responses.  Defense counsel requested an extension to September 1, 2026 to provide responses without objections.  They claimed that the failure to provide responses was due to a scheduling error.  (Ex. A to Opp.)   

Plaintiff’s counsel agreed to an extension to August 14, 2026.  Defendants did not provide responses by August 14, 2026.  They provided responses on September 2, 2026, which is one day after their own requested extension date.   

This hearing is on Plaintiff’s four motions to compel responses to Form Interrogatories (Set One) (“FROGs”), Special Interrogatories (Set One) (“SROGs”), Document Demands (Set One) (“RFPs”), motion to deem admitted Requests for Admissions (“RFAs”) and request for sanctions.   

LEGAL STANDARD 

A motion to compel an initial response can be made on the ground that a party did not serve a timely response.  (Code Civ. Proc., § 2030.290, subd. (a), § 2031 subd. (a) and (b); see¿Sinaiko Healthcare Consulting, Inc. v. Pacific Healthcare Consultants (2007) 148 Cal.App.4th 390, 404.)¿¿ Failing to timely respond waives any objections. (CCP § 2030.290(a).)¿ 

To move to compel initial responses, a movant must show: (1) proper service (see¿Code Civ. Proc., § 2030.080, subd. (a)); (2) expiration of the deadline for the initial response, 30 days after service or on date agreed to by the parties (see¿Code Civ. Proc., § 2030.260, subds. (a),¿(b)); and (3) no timely response (see¿Code Civ. Proc., § 2030.90).¿ 

There is no “meet and confer” requirement where there is a total failure to respond to discovery.¿ (Sinaiko, 148 Cal.App.4th at 411.)¿ There is also no separate statement requirement for a motion to compel initial responses.¿ (Cal. Rules of Court Rule 3.1345(b).)¿ 

Where the court grants a motion to compel responses, sanctions shall be imposed against a party, person, or attorney who unsuccessfully makes or opposes a motion to compel, unless the person or entity acted with substantial justification or the sanction would otherwise be unjust. (Code Civ. Proc., §§ 2030.290, 2031.90, 2033.280, subds. (c);¿Cal. Rule of Court, rule 3.1348.)¿ 

In addition, the court may award sanctions for any misuse of discovery process.¿ (Code Civ. Proc. §§ 2023.010¿and¿2023.030.)¿ A failure to timely respond constitutes a misuse of the discovery process.¿ (Code Civ. Proc, § 2023.010, subd. (d).)¿¿ 

DISCUSSION 

Interrogatories 

Code Civ. Proc. § 2030.290(a) provides that if a party fails to serve a timely response to served interrogatories, that party waives any objections, and the propounding party may move for an order compelling responses thereto.  Defendant’s responses to Plaintiff’s FROGs and SROGs were due by December 30, 2025.  Plaintiff granted an extension to August 14, 2026 so long as the responses did not contain objections.  Defendant belatedly served its responses on September 2, 2026.  Accordingly, the motion to compel responses to the interrogatories is moot.  

Document Demands 

Code Civ. Proc. § 2031.300 (a) and (b) provides that if a party fails to serve a timely response to a demand for production, that party waives any right to serve objections to the demand, including ones based on privilege or work product protection, and the propounding party may move for an order compelling responses thereto.  Defendant’s responses to Plaintiff’s RFPs were originally due by December 30, 2025.  Plaintiff extended the deadline to August 14, 2026.  Defendant served its late responses on September 2, 2026.  Accordingly, the motion to compel responses to the RFPs is now moot.   

Requests for Admissions 

Where a party fails to timely respond to a request for admission, the propounding party may move for an order that the genuineness of any documents and the truth of any matters specified in the requests be deemed admitted.  (Code Civ. Proc., § 2033.280, subd. (b).)  The party who failed to respond waives any objections to the demand, unless the court grants them relief from the waiver, upon a showing that the party (1) has subsequently served a substantially compliant response, and (2) that the party’s failure to respond was the result of mistake, inadvertence, or excusable neglect.  (Code Civ. Proc., § 2033.280, subds. (a)(1)-(2).) 

Here, Plaintiff’s responses to Defendant’s RFAs were due by December 30, 2025.  Defendant did not serve responses until September 2, 2026.  Accordingly, Defendant is deemed to have admitted the requests for admissions unless they can show that the September 2 responses they served were “substantially compliant” and that their failure to timely respond was the result of mistake, inadvertence or excusable neglect.   

Defendant submitted a declaration from its counsel who does not explain the failure to timely respond.  Instead, Defendant’s opposition attempts to shift blame to Plaintiff for alerting counsel to Defendant’s duty to respond, months after the responses were due, and refusing to extend Defendant’s time to respond for an additional 30 days.  None of these facts explain why Defendant failed to timely respond.  Plaintiff is not obligated to remind Defendant of its deadline to respond to discovery requests.  Nor is Plaintiff required to provide extensions to Defendant.   

In addition, Defendant’s counsel attests that responses to the RFAs were served on September 2, 2026.  The responses are not attached to the opposition, and Defendant has not shown that the responses are substantially compliant.  Indeed, defense counsel does not even attest in his/her declaration that the responses are substantially compliant.   

Defendant attempts to excuse its failure to timely respond by arguing that Plaintiff is not prejudiced because trial is in January 2028.  But prejudice is not a requirement on a motion to deem RFAs admitted.  And the fact that trial is in 2028 does not mean that Defendant can just ignore a discovery request.  Accordingly, the Court deems the RFAs admitted by 655 Kenton LP. 

Sanctions 

Regardless of the reason or excuse for the delay in responding to RFAs, it is¿mandatory¿that the court impose a monetary sanction on a party whose¿failure¿to¿timely respond¿to the RFAs necessitated the motion.¿ (Appleton v. Superior Court (1988) 206 Cal.App.3d 632, 634;¿Code Civ. Proc., § 2033.280(c).)  While delayed responses may avoid a motion to deem admitted, they will not avoid monetary sanctions.  (Code Civ. Proc., § 2033.280 subd. (c);¿Gonzales v. Harris, 2021 Cal. Super. LEXIS 29267 at *6¿(even if delayed responses are served, sanctions are mandatory because the motion had to be brought, regardless of whether it is ultimately denied because responses are served before the hearing).) 

Further, the Court may also impose sanctions for the failure to timely respond to the FROGs, SROGs and RFPs.  Code Civ. Proc. § 2030.290 states: “The court shall impose a monetary sanction under Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 2023.010) against any party, person, or attorney who unsuccessfully makes or opposes a motion to compel a response to interrogatories, unless it finds that the one subject to the sanction acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust.” 

Likewise, Code of Civil Procedure § 2031.300 states: “(c) Except as provided in subdivision (d), the court shall impose a monetary sanction under Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 2023.010) against any party, person, or attorney who unsuccessfully makes or opposes a motion to compel a response to a demand for inspection, copying, testing, or sampling, unless it finds that the one subject to the sanction acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust.” 

Although §§ 2030.290 and 2031.300 impose sanctions only when a party unsuccessfully makes or opposes a motion to compel, Local Rule 3.1348 allows the Court to impose sanctions “in favor of a party who files a motion to compel discovery, even though no opposition to the motion was filed, or opposition to the motion was withdrawn, or the requested discovery was provided to the moving party after the motion was filed.” 

Moreover, the Court may award sanctions for discovery abuses which include the failure to timely respond to discovery.  (Code Civ. Proc., §§¿2023.010 subd. (d),¿2023.030).)  “Courts are authorized to exercise their discretion to award discovery sanctions for abuse of the discovery process.”  (NewLife Sciences, LLC v. Weinstock (2011) 197 Cal.App.4th 676, fn. 10 (citing Code Civ. Proc., §§¿2023.010,¿2023.030).) 

The Court concludes that sanctions are warranted given Defendant’s failure to timely respond.  In determining the appropriate amount of sanctions, the Court¿starts¿with the¿lodestar¿which is the reasonable hourly rate multiplied by the reasonable hours spent.¿ (PLCM Group v. Drexler (2000) 22 Cal.4th 1084, 1096; see also¿Ketchum v. Moses (2001) 24 Cal.4th 1122, 1132.)   

Plaintiff’s counsel (Robert Booker) seeks an hourly rate is $1000.  He has been practicing law for over 20 years.  He was a partner at his prior firm and is the senior managing attorney of his current firm (The Law Offices of Jacob Emrani).  He is a graduate of Pepperdine Law School. 

Mr. Booker’s declaration does not provide any support for his requested rate, other than his 20+ years practicing as a lawyer.  There is no indication that his $1000 requested hourly rate was approved by any court; there is no declaration from an attorney at a different firm attesting to the hourly rates of personal injury lawyers with 20+ years experience, and Mr. Booker does not provide any third party report or survey (e.g., the Real Rate Report) that would shed light on prevailing market rates for attorneys with experiences and backgrounds similar to his.  Accordingly, the Court will award sanctions based on a $500 hourly rate.   

As to the hours spent on the motion, Plaintiff seeks four hours as to each motion, two hours to draft the motion and prepare the supporting documentation, one hour to prepare a reply, and one hour to prepare for and attend the hearing.  As there is only one hearing on all four motions, the Court will only award an hour total for time to prepare for and attend the hearing.  As to the other hours, the Court concludes they are reasonable. 

Plaintiff also seeks costs in the amount of $60 for each motion.  The costs are for filing fees.  The Court concludes that these costs are also reasonable. 

In sum, the Court will award fees of and costs of $6,740 (3 x $500 x 4 + $240).   

CONCLUSION 

Based on the foregoing, the Court DENIES IN PART and GRANTS IN PART Defendant’s motions to compel and request for sanctions.  The Court will award sanctions in the amount of $6,740 jointly and severally against Defendant and its counsel.   

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.

Edward B. Moreton, Jr. 

Judge of the Superior Court 

Case Number: 25SMCV05446    Hearing Date: September 23, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

NIKKI RAHEJA,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

THE DAILY PINT, INC., et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 25SMCV05446 

  Hearing Date:  September 23, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  defendant WORLDWIDE DISCOVERY 

  CORP.’s DEMURRER TO AND MOTION  

  TO STRIKE COMPLAINT  

 

 

  

 

BACKGROUND 

This is an employment retaliation case.  Plaintiff Nikki Raheja is a bartender.  She also operates her own marketing agency and dance studio.  Defendant The Daily Pint, Inc. owns and operates a bar and restaurant at 2310 Pico Boulevard, called the Daily Pint.  Plaintiff also alleges that Defendants Worldwide Discovery Corp. and Bar on Pico, LLC, own, operate, manage and/or control the Daily Pint. 

According to the Complaint, on June 11, 2024, Plaintiff applied for an open bartending position at the Daily Pint.  Plaintiff interviewed with the Bar Manager, Manny.  Manny offered Plaintiff the bartending position on the spot, and Plaintiff verbally accepted the job offer.  Plaintiff never formally began employment; the job offer was made and accepted but then revoked before Plaintiff's start date.  

In the early morning hours of June 14, 2024, Jose Hernandez, a frequent patron and close associate of Manny, followed Plaintiff home under the pretense of talking to her about the bartending position. While at Plaintiff's home, Hernandez gave Plaintiff a drink which she believes was drugged.  Hernandez made unwanted sexual advances toward Plaintiff.  When Plaintiff rejected his advances, Hernandez physically assaulted Plaintiff.  As Hernandez left Plaintiff's home, he threatened Plaintiff’s job saying: “Good luck with the job now”. 

Plaintiff filed a police report against Hernandez.  Santa Monica police detectives told Plaintiff that Hernandez is involved in organized criminal activity.  Plaintiff claims that in making the report, she engaged in protected activity under Labor Code section 6310 because she reported unsafe working conditions that posed a direct threat to employee safety and violated occupational safety and health standards.  

After filing the police report, Plaintiff returned to The Daily Pint to talk to Manny.  When Plaintiff reported the sexual assault to Manny, he made clear that the job offer was being revoked in direct retaliation for Plaintiff's rejection of Hernandez’s sexual advances and for Plaintiff's filing a police report.  Manny specifically told Plaintiff, “you messed with my friend so it’s done.”   

On July 7, 2024, Defendants officially revoked the job offer and hired another person for the job.  Plaintiff claims that the person hired (Maggie Powers) was significantly less qualified than her.  

After her police report, Plaintiff claims that Defendants’ harassment escalated.  Plaintiff alleges that Manny, Hernandez, and other individuals connected to Defendants’ bar targeted her dance studio clients, damaging her business relationships and discouraging her clients from attending her classes.  Plaintiff’s claims her dance class enrollments have decreased as students and their families feared association with Plaintiff.  

Defendants also damaged Plaintiff’s marketing business by warning patrons not to associate or do business with her, and instructing customers and patrons, “don’t talk to her, don’t do business with her.”  As a direct result of Defendants’ campaign to damage Plaintiff’s professional reputation, Plaintiff’s marketing agency clients declined to work with her due to fear of retaliation from Hernandez and his associates.   

The harassment included threatening phone calls at all hours, including one placed from the bar’s business line.  Defendants and their agents called Plaintiff a “rat” and subjected her to death threats and intimidation.  They also referred to her as a “Jesus freak” and mocked her Christian faith and celibate lifestyle.  The new bartender (Maggie) physically assaulted Plaintiff as she was walking by the bar.   

On June 16, 2025, Plaintiff’s counsel made written requests to Defendants for Plaintiff’s personnel records pursuant to Labor Code section 1198.5 and payroll records pursuant to Labor Code section 226(b). The statutory deadlines for production of these records have elapsed, and Defendants have failed to provide the requested records to Plaintiff.   

Plaintiff alleges that the corporate Defendants are vicariously liable for all acts of harassment, retaliation, intimidation, and other unlawful conduct committed by their agents, employees, managers, representatives, patrons, and associates because they authorized, knew of, ratified, participated in, or failed to prevent the conduct.  

The operative second amended complaint (“SAC”) alleges claims for (1) Whistleblower Retaliation in Violation of Labor Code § 1102.5; (2) Retaliation for Reporting Unsafe Conditions in Violation of Labor Code § 6310; (3) Failure to Produce Payroll Records in Violation of Labor Code § 226(b); (4) Failure to Produce Personnel File in Violation of Labor Code § 1198.5; and (5) Interference with Prospective Economic Relations (IPER).   

This hearing is on Worldwide Discovery Corp.’s demurrer and motion to strike.  Worldwide argues that Plaintiff cannot prove retaliation because she has not alleged she was employed by Worldwide, and she has not alleged any protected activity.  Her report about an assault was not a report of unsafe working conditions because it occurred at her home, and not at the Daily Pint.  As to the claim for failure to produce employment records, Worldwide argues that it lacks sufficient detail as to where the request was made.  As to the interference claim, Worldwide argues that Plaintiff has not alleged any economic relationships of which Worldwide was aware or that Worldwide engaged in any wrongful act.   

As to its motion to strike, Worldwide argues that Plaintiff’s claim for punitive damages fails because it has not alleged malice, oppression or fraud on the part of Worldwide.  Worldwide also seeks to strike Plaintiff’s request for statutory penalties, the reference to a right to sue letter that was not attached, and a placeholder for the name of Plaintiff’s dance studio.  

MEET AND CONFER 

Code Civ. Proc. §§ 430.41 and 435.5 requires that before the filing of a demurrer or motion to strike, the moving party “shall meet and confer in person or by telephone” with the party who filed the pleading that is subject to demurrer or motion to strike for the purpose of determining whether an agreement can be reached that would resolve the objections to be raised in the demurrer or motion to strike.  (Code Civ. Proc., §§ 430.41(a), 435.5(a).)  The parties are to meet and confer at least five days before the date the responsive pleading is due. (Code Civ. Proc., §§ 430.41(a)(2), 435.5(a)(2).)  Thereafter, the moving party shall file and serve a declaration detailing their meet and confer efforts. (Code Civ. Proc., §§ 430.41(a)(3), 435.5(a)(3).)  Worldwide submits the Declaration of Danielle Little who attests that the parties met and conferred by telephone.  This satisfies Worldwide’s meet and confer obligations.   

LEGAL STANDARD 

“[A] demurrer tests the legal sufficiency of the allegations in a complaint.” (Lewis v. Safeway, Inc. (2015) 235 Cal.App.4th 385, 388.)  A demurrer can be used only to challenge defects that appear on the face of the pleading under attack or from matters outside the pleading that are judicially noticeable.  (See Donabedian v. Mercury Ins. Co. (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 968, 994 (in ruling on a demurrer, a court may not consider declarations, matters not subject to judicial notice, or documents not accepted for the truth of their contents).)  For purposes of ruling on a demurrer, all facts pleaded in a complaint are assumed to be true, but the reviewing court does not assume the truth of conclusions of law. (Aubry v. Tri-City Hosp. Dist. (1992) 2 Cal.4th 962, 967.)  

Further, the court may, upon motion, or at any time in its discretion, and upon terms it deems proper, strike any irrelevant, false, or improper matter inserted in any pleading.  (Code Civ. Proc., § 436, subd. (a).)  The court may also strike all or any part of any pleading not drawn or filed in conformity with the laws of this state, a court rule, or an order of the court. (Code Civ. Proc., § 436, subd. (b).)  The grounds for a motion to strike are that the pleading has irrelevant, false, or improper matter, or has not been drawn or filed in conformity with laws.  (Code Civ. Proc., § 436.)  The grounds for moving to strike must appear on the face of the pleading or by way of judicial notice. (Code Civ. Proc., § 437.) 

Leave to amend must be allowed where there is a reasonable possibility of successful amendment. (See Goodman v. Kennedy (1976) 18 Cal.3d 335, 349 (court shall not “sustain a demurrer without leave to amend if there is any reasonable possibility that the defect can be cured by amendment”); Kong v. City of Hawaiian Gardens Redevelopment Agency (2002) 108 Cal.App.4th 1028, 1037 (“A demurrer should not be sustained without leave to amend if the complaint, liberally construed, can state a cause of action under any theory or if there is a reasonable possibility the defect can be cured by amendment.”); Vaccaro v. Kaiman (1998) 63 Cal.App.4th 761, 768 (“When the defect which justifies striking a complaint is capable of cure, the court should allow leave to amend.”).)  The burden is on the complainant to show the Court that a pleading can be amended successfully. (Blank v. Kirwan (1985) 39 Cal.3d 311, 318.) 

DISCUSSION 

Whistleblower Retaliation 

To plead a prima facie case of “whistleblower” retaliation under Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5, Plaintiff must allege facts that, if true, satisfy the following elements: (1) Worldwide was her employer; (2) she engaged in protected activity; (3) she experienced an adverse employment action; and (4) a causal link exists between the protected activity and adverse action.  (See Judicial Council of California Civil Jury Instruction 4603; St. Myers v. Dignity Health, 44 Cal. App. 5th 301, 314, 257 Cal. Rptr. 3d 341 (2019)). 

Worldwide argues that Plaintiff has not alleged she had an employment relationship with Worldwide.  The Court agrees.   

Paragraph 7 of the Complaint states that “Bar Manager Manny (last name unknown) was an employee of Defendant Daily Pint with actual authority to make hiring decisions on behalf of Defendant Daily Pint, acted as Plaintiff's supervisor, made decisions regarding the job offer extended to Plaintiff on behalf of Defendant Daily Pint, and exercised sufficient managerial control over hiring and employment decisions to bind Defendant Daily Pint. Bar Manager Manny's actions were within the course and scope of his employment and were ratified by Defendant Daily Pint.”  In other words, Plaintiff’s employment relationship was formed with Daily Pint, not Worldwide. 

Of course, Plaintiff alleges that Worldwide is a “joint employer.”  However, this is merely a conclusion which the Court is not required to accept as true on a demurrer.   

In assessing whether there is an employment relationship, the Court looks to several factors including the payment of salary or other employment benefits and Social Security taxes, the ownership of the equipment necessary to performance of the job, the location where the work is performed, the obligation of the defendant to train the employee, the authority of the defendant to hire, transfer, promote, discipline or discharge the employee, the authority to establish work schedules and assignments, the defendant’s discretion to determine the amount of compensation earned by the employee, the skill required of the work performed and the extent to which it is done under the direction of a supervisor, whether the work is part of the defendant’s regular business operations, the skill required in the particular occupation, the duration of the relationship of the parties, and the duration of the plaintiff’s employment.  (Vernon v. State of California (2004) 116 Cal.App.4th 114, 125.) 

“Of these factors, the extent of the defendant’s right to control the means and manner of the workers’ performance is the most important.”  (Id. at 126.)  Further, “the control an organization asserts must be ‘significant,’ [citation], and there must be a ‘sufficient indicia of an interrelationship … to justify the belief on the part of an aggrieved employee that the [alleged co-employer] is jointly responsible for the acts of the immediate employer.”  (Id.)   

Here, there is no allegation that Worldwide had any control, much less significant control, over the means and manner of Plaintiff’s work.  Indeed, according to Plaintiff, she never worked at Daily Pint, because her job offer was rescinded before she started work.   

Plaintiff also alleges that Worldwide is an alter ego of Daily Pint.  This allegation is conclusory as well.   

“Two requirements must be met to invoke the alter ego doctrine: (1) '[T]here must be such a unity of interest and ownership between the corporation and its equitable owner that the separate personalities of the corporation and the shareholder do not in reality exist'; and (2) 'there must be an inequitable result if the acts in question are treated as those of the corporation alone.' [Citation.]” (Turman v. Superior Court (2017) 17 Cal.App.5th 969, 980-981.) In addition to these two elements, the Court of Appeal in Greenspan v. LADT, LLC (2010) 191 Cal.App. 4th 486, 512-513 specifies 15 non-exhaustive factors that one should plead in support of the alter ego doctrine.  The SAC does not contain any allegations to support either element of the alter ego doctrine.   

Accordingly, because Plaintiff has not alleged an employment relationship with Worldwide, the Court sustains the demurrer to her whistleblower retaliation claim.   

Reporting Unsafe Conditions 

Plaintiff alleges she was retaliated against for reporting unsafe working conditions in violation of Lab. Code section 6310.  Worldwide argues that Plaintiff’s report to the police and to Manny was not about working conditions, but about an assault that occurred at her home.  In opposition, Plaintiff argues that California courts “have squarely held that complaints about dangerous individuals who have access to the workplace, including coworkers, clients, customers, patients, and other third parties, constitute protected activity under § 6310 when the employee reasonably believes the individual poses a credible threat of violence or physical harm in the workplace.” 

Before addressing the parties’ arguments, the Court notes that Labor Code section 6310(a)(1) only applies to reports to “the division, other governmental agencies having statutory responsibility for or assisting the division with reference to employee safety or health, their employer, or their representative.”  Plaintiff’s complaint to the Santa Monica police department, therefore, does not count as the SMPD is not a governmental agency charged with assisting the Labor Commissioner with employee safety or health.  The only relevant complaint for purposes of section 6310 is Plaintiff’s complaint to Manny. 

Further, section 6310 provides that “no person shall discharge or in any manner discriminate against any employee” so the statute seems to extend beyond employers.  The court has not found any California authorities as to the meaning of “person” in section 6310.  Federal courts (interpreting section 6310) have held that it also extends to individual supervisors.  (De La Torre v. Progress Rail Servs. Corp., No. CV 15-4526-FMO (GJSx), 2015 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 100784, 2015 WL 4607730, at *5 (C.D. Cal. July 31, 2015); Boone v. Carlsbad Cmty. Church, No. 08-CV-0634 W (AJB), 2008 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 44675, 2008 WL 2357238, at *7 (S.D. Cal. June 6, 2008). But the Court has not found any cases (federal or otherwise) that have applied section 6310 to “persons” other than employers or supervisors.   

As discussed above, the Complaint does not contain sufficient allegations to support the conclusory claim that Worldwide is Plaintiff’s employer.  Further, while Plaintiff alleges that Worldwide was her supervisor (SAC ¶ 3), this conclusory allegation is not supported by any facts.   

In the context of FEHA, a “supervisor” is someone who has authority to hire, transfer, promote, assign, reward, discipline or discharge other employees, has the responsibility to act on other employees’ grievances or effectively to recommend action on grievances; or the responsibility to direct other employees’ daily work activities.  (CACI No. 2525.)  The alleged supervisor’s exercise of this authority or responsibility must not be “merely routine or clerical, but must require the use of independent judgment.”  (Id.)  There are no facts alleged in the Complaint that Worldwide had any of these powers or responsibilities. 

Accordingly, the Court need not address whether the complaint to Manny was about worker safety because section 6310 does not apply to Worldwide, under the current allegations in Plaintiff’s complaint.  Therefore, the Court sustains the demurrer to the section 6310 claim.   

Failure to Produce Payroll/Personnel Records 

Plaintiff has sued Worldwide for violations of California Labor Code §§ 226(b) and 1198.5.  Section 226(b) requires an employer to comply with a request by a current or former employee to inspect or receive “a copy of records pertaining to their employment.”  The failure by an employer to comply within 21 days of the request “entitles the current or former employee or the Labor Commissioner to recover a seven-hundred-fifty-dollar ($750) penalty from the employer.”  (Id.§ 226(f).)  The employee may also seek injunctive relief.  (Id.) 

Comparably, California Labor Code section 1198.5 affords “[e]very current and former employee . . . the right to inspect and receive a copy of the personnel records that the employer maintains relating to the employee’s performance or to any grievance concerning the employee.” (Cal. Lab. Code § 1198.5(a).) An employer is required to make these records available within "30 calendar days from the date the employer receives a written request." Id.§ 1198.5(b). The failure to comply with this requirement, similar to section 226, entitles the requesting party to “recover a penalty of seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) from the employer” and to bring an action for injunctive relief to obtain compliance with this section, and may recover costs and reasonable attorney's fees in such an action.”  (Id.§ 1198.5(k)—(l).) 

Because the Court concludes that the SAC does not sufficiently allege that Worldwide is Plaintiff’s employer, neither of these claims can be asserted against Worldwide.  Accordingly, the Court sustains the demurrer to the third and fourth causes of action. 

Interference with Prospective Economic Advantage 

Intentional interference with prospective economic advantage has five elements: (1) the existence, between the plaintiff and some third party, of an economic relationship that contains the probability of future economic benefit to the plaintiff; (2) the defendant’s knowledge of the relationship; (3) intentionally wrongful acts designed to disrupt the relationship; (4) actual disruption of the relationship; and (5) economic harm proximately caused by the defendant's action. (Korea Supply, 29 Cal.4th at pp. 1164–1165.) 

The first element has two parts: (1) an existing economic relationship that (2) contains the probability of an economic benefit to the plaintiff.  Here, Plaintiff has sufficiently alleged the existence of an economic relationship between herself and her dance/marketing clients.  She is not required to provide their specific names at the pleading stage.  (See Ramona Manor Convalescent Hosp. v. Care Enters., 177 Cal. App. 3d 1120, 1127-28 (1986) (the specific name of the third party need not be alleged to recover for an interference claim, although that party must be "identified in some manner") 

As to the second element, Plaintiff alleges that “Defendants” had knowledge of her business relationships and economic interests because her dance studio is located 500 feet from the bar, and “Plaintiff operated her businesses in the same community where Defendants conduct business.”  While these allegations are thin, the Court concludes they are sufficient at the pleading stage.   

As to the third element, Plaintiff alleges that “Defendants” interfered with her prospective economic relations “by spreading Plaintiff's name throughout The Daily Pint establishment and instructing customers and patrons ‘don't talk to her, don't do business with her.’” Defendants also allegedly engaged in “harassment and intimidation tactics that created fear among Plaintiff's clients and students of potential gang retaliation from Jose Hernandez and his associates.” 

The only persons identified by name as engaging in this harassment are Manny and Maggie.  However, there are no specific facts alleged to suggest they are the agents of Worldwide.  Rather, they are identified as employees of Daily Pint.  And their alleged connection to Worldwide is via Plaintiff’s conclusory allegations of alter ego or joint employer.  As discussed above, the allegations are insufficient to support a finding that Worldwide is a joint employer or alter ego.   

Accordingly, because Plaintiff has not alleged facts to support the third element, the Court sustains the demurrer as to the interference claim as well.  

CONCLUSION AND ORDER 

Based on the foregoing, the Court SUSTAINS the demurrer with 20 days’ leave to amend.  The Court denies the motion to strike as moot.

  PLAINTIFF’S MOTION TO QUASH  

  DEPOSITION SUBPOENA  

  issued by defendantS to AMTRUST     NORTH AMERICA, INC. 

 

  

 

 

 

 

 

This is a negligence and premises liability case.  Plaintiff claims that while he was a lawful guest on Defendants’ property, a gate or fence fell on him, causing injuries.  Plaintiff alleges that Defendants failed to properly maintain the gate/fence. 

This hearing is on Plaintiff’s motion to quash a deposition subpoena issued by Defendants to Amtrust North America, Inc. in c/o United Agent Group Inc. (the “Subpoena”).  The Subpoena seeks “any and all” of Plaintiff’s worker’s compensation records, including but not limited to, claim files, medical records, medical billing, and benefit records.  Plaintiff argues that the Subpoena is overly broad and invades his constitutional right to privacy. 

This Department’s rules require that on a discovery motion, the parties must meet and confer to informally resolve their dispute, and when that fails, the parties must attend an informal discovery conference (IDC).  There is no record of an IDC on the issues raised in Plaintiff’s motion to quash.  Accordingly, the Court denies the motion to quash without prejudice.   

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.
